r.정치 구도: Malaysia is a federal constitutional monarchy in which the hereditary rulers of nine states take turns electing a king every five years. Day-to-day politics is run by a prime minister backed by a majority in parliament, but when no side wins a majority the king holds the key to choosing who governs. After independence in 1957, the same ruling coalition held power for 61 years until it lost in 2018 amid public anger over the 1MDB state investment fund scandal. Defections then brought down governments in quick succession, prompting a 2022 law banning lawmakers from switching parties; the election that year produced no majority, and former rivals joined forces in a unity government. The Bumiputera policies favoring Malays and indigenous groups, questions of race and religion, and demands for more autonomy from the Borneo states of Sabah and Sarawak are the big political fault lines.

t.why: Together with Singapore and Indonesia it lines the Strait of Malacca, which links the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea and carries a large share of the oil and cargo bound for China, Japan and South Korea. Built up over more than half a century around Penang, its chip assembly and testing industry handles about 13% of the world's semiconductor back-end work, and companies looking to relocate amid the US-China chip rivalry are flocking in. As the world's second-largest palm oil producer after Indonesia, it pushed back hard against an EU regulation barring imports of goods linked to deforestation. Its claims in the South China Sea overlap with China's, but it prefers quiet diplomacy to confrontation. It chaired ASEAN in 2025 and hosted the summit in Kuala Lumpur.
t.rel: It shares sea and land borders with Singapore, Indonesia and Brunei. Its claims in the South China Sea overlap with China's, but it mostly opts for quiet diplomacy, and it has a long-running dispute with the Philippines over Sabah.
t.korea: The two countries established diplomatic relations in 1960. In 1982 the then prime minister launched the Look East policy, urging Malaysians to learn from the industry and work ethic of Japan and South Korea, and many Malaysian students and trainees went to Korea. The Penang Bridge, opened in 1985, was built by Hyundai Engineering & Construction, and from around that time Korean builders took on many of Malaysia's big projects. Korean companies also have major production bases there, including Samsung SDI's battery plant in Seremban and Lotte Chemical's petrochemical subsidiary in Johor. Ties were upgraded to a strategic partnership in 2024, and the two sides announced the conclusion of free trade agreement negotiations in October 2025.
t.know: The Petronas Twin Towers in Kuala Lumpur were once the world's tallest buildings, and one of the two towers was built by a Korean construction company.
etext: Global chipmakers such as Intel and Infineon run plants in Penang and Kulim that package and test chips. The government wants to move up from assembly into chip design and advanced packaging.

State oil company Petronas develops oil and gas off Sarawak and Sabah, exports liquefied natural gas and supplies a large share of government revenue. Palm oil comes from plantations on the peninsula and in Borneo, relies heavily on migrant workers and is dogged by controversy over deforestation.
Johor, next to Singapore, has ample power and land, and large data centers are going up fast. Because they consume so much electricity and water, the government is tightening its investment criteria.

The country has been stuck at middle income for a long time, and raising wages and productivity is the challenge. Talent drains to Singapore and elsewhere, and critics say preferential policies for indigenous groups hold back business competition.
